latin: Poppaedius<sup>1</sup> nauta, cum in scapha remigaret, ecce repente marinum draconem<sup>2</sup> respexit.
Poppaedius. — Mehercule! Quam horribile monstrum!
Monstrum, Poppaedium, qui non summa erat pulchritudine, inspiciens. — Eadem tibi dicturus fui<sup>3</sup>!
Senex. — Tuane est haec sagitta?
Puer. — Quid fractum est?
Senex. — Nihil fractum est.
Puer. — Bene, mea sagitta est.
Cosinus, physicus peritissimus, de bestiolarum<sup>4</sup> moribus motibusque inquirebat.
In laboratorio suo muscas, formicas, locustas, cimices<sup>5</sup>, pediculos, etc., alebat.
Quondam pulicem<sup>6</sup> condocefactum<sup>7</sup> cum descriptione a magistro data, accepit.
Ex hac descriptione, quibus vocibus bestiola oboediret<sup>8</sup> scire potuit.
Experimentum primum paravit. Cum vir esset doctus et methodicus, eventa omnia in chartis idoneis notabat.
Omnibus rebus in suis locis positis, pulici imperavit: «Exsili<sup>9</sup>!».
Pulex exsiluit. Cosinus eventum<sup>10</sup> in commentariis<sup>11</sup> notavit.
Deinde artis chirurgicae, in qua olim se exercuerat, memor, pulicis cruscula<sup>12</sup> desecuit<sup>13</sup> et experimentum alterum paravit.
Iterum pulici: «Exsili!» imperavit. Pulex autem non exsiluit.
In commentariis notare non dubitavit:
«Cruribus abscisis<sup>14</sup>, pulex obsurdescit<sup>15</sup>».
english: Popeye the sailor, while he was rowing in a boat, suddenly [saw] behind him a sea serpent.
Popeye. — By Hercules! What a horrible monster!
The monster, examining Popeye, who was not of the most perfect beauty. — I was going to say the same thing to you!
The old gentleman. — Is this arrow yours?
The little boy. — What has been broken?
The old gentleman. — Nothing has been broken.
The little boy. — Well then, it's my arrow.
Cosinus, very experienced naturalist, was studying the customs and [reflexes] (movements) of insects (little beasts).
In his laboratory, [he raised] flies, ants, grasshoppers, bugs, lice, etc. (nourished).
One day he received a learned flea with an instruction leaflet given by the trainer.
With this leaflet, he could know to which words the little beast obeyed.
He prepared a first experiment. As he was a learned and methodical man, he noted all the events on appropriate papers.
All (things) having been put in (their own) place, he said to the flea: «Jump!».
The flea jumped. The naturalist noted the event in his registers.
Then, remembering the surgical art in which he had formerly practised, he cut off the flea's legs and prepared a second experiment.
He said again to the flea: «Jump!». But the flea did not jump.
He [did not hesitate to note] in his register:
«After its legs have been cut off, the flea becomes deaf».

footnotes: Poppaedius, -ii, m., Popeye, character of numerous English animated drawings, is also known in France under the nickname of Mathurin. He feeds (vescor, -eris, -i) exclusively on spinach (spinacia, -ae, f.) from which he draws his legendary strength: Poppaedius spinaciis solis vescitur unde vires suas fabulosas trahit.

Draco, -onis, m., the serpent or the dragon. Draco, proper name, is also the Drac, tributary of the Isère. Serpent is also said serpens, -entis, m. (pres. part. of serpo, -is, -ere, serpsi, v.i., to crawl).
Dicturus fui: with the future participle and the past of the auxiliary one obtains THE FUTURE IN THE PAST.
Bestiola, -ae, f., diminutive of bestia, -ae, f., the beast (as opposed to man, whereas animal is opposed to plants and minerals).
Cimex, -icis, m., the bug; no difficulty for finding the declension of the other «little beasts» of P. 9.
Pulex, -icis, m., the flea. Note, as for cimex, the MASCULINE gender.

Condocefactus, perfect participle of condocefieri which serves as passive to condocefacere, to train (from docere). One could have said: mansuetus, -a, -um, tamed, gentle, benevolent (mansuetudo, the fact of being tamed, gentleness, meekness; mansuefacere, to tame; mansuefieri, to be tamed; mansuetarius, he who tames, the tamer) if it had been a question of a bestia and not of a bestiola.
Oboedio or obedio, -is, -ire, ivi or ii, itum (ob audire), to lend an ear, whence to obey. Here in the imperfect subjunctive (cf. R. and N. 98, § 2. B. 2°).
Exsilire is more precise than salire which we could have used strictly. If you have forgotten the latter, see above L. 80, N. 10.
If you do not know from which verb eventum comes, see above L. 62, N. 14.
Commentarius, -ii, m., book of notes, register, historical memoir (commentary) and even review (periodical). One also says commentarium, -ii, n.
Crusculum, -i, n., diminutive of crus, cruris, n., the leg (the paw) for it is a question of a small beast.

Desecuit: do not forget that the verbs of the 1st conjugation do not all make the perfect in avi and the supine in atum. Thus seco, -as, -are, secui, sectum, to cut, to slice (cf. L. 23, P. 2), and its compounds desecare, to separate by cutting and dissecare, to divide by cutting, to dissect.

Abscido, -is, -ere, scidi, scisum, to remove by cutting; there also exists abscindo, -is, -ere, scidi, scissum. Pronounce well the two s's of the supine of this last, to distinguish it from the first.
Obsurdesco, -is, -ere, surdui, inchoative verb (R. and N. 3. D.) to become deaf (surdus, -a, -um); mute is said mutus, -a, -um and blind you have already seen (caecus).
comments: Remark. — For reasons of vocabulary, we have permitted ourselves to modify and to increase the original text. On the other hand this adventure is attributed by Acta Diurna to a certain Fulvius. We think, for our part, that it must be attributed to Zephyrinus Brioché, better known under the name of Savant Cosinus, and whose Christophe has related the moving experiments. This scientist being absent-minded, it is to be feared that he forgot to immortalize his works in the language that we are studying. May this gap be filled in the best delays, and this appeal to goodwill not be lost!
EXERCISE. — In this last exercise we will continue to read, to the end, these extracts from Frontinus, of which we saw the 1st part in lesson 99 (nonagesima nona).

Quinaria (understood fistula), the pipe called of 5 (quini, -ae, -a, 5 by 5), that is to say, according to Frontinus, which has 5/4 of an inch in diameter. The flow of such a pipe was the unit of measure employed for the distribution of water: water meters had not yet been invented. — Erogare (ex rogare), to spend; here to take water (by any conduit) to distribute it (by more or less small pipes). — Patrimonium, -ii, n. (from pater), what one has as father of family, the patrimony. Other derivatives in monium: matrimonium, marriage (from mater); testimonium, testimony (testis, -is, m., the witness), etc. — Detego, -is, -ere, texi, tectum (de + tegere, cf. L. 48, P. 11), to uncover, to detect. — Modus, -i, m., measure. — Intercido, -is, -ere, cidi (inter + cadere), to fall between (i short). — Temperare, to combine, to arrange, to organize, to moderate. Note that dum, when it signifies as much as, is constructed with the indicative, and often with the indicative PRESENT, whatever the real time of the subordinate. — Fraus, fraudis, f., ruse of bad faith, fraud. — Aquarius, -a, -um, relating to water. Aquarius, taken as a noun, designates the man who occupies himself with water, the fountain-maker. The corresponding neuter substantive, aquarium (reservoir), gave the French évier. — Deprehendo, -is, -ere, di, sum, to stop, to take (prehendere, same conjugation) in passing. — Plerique (f. pleraeque, n. pleraque), the majority, is used as an adjective. — Inriguus or irriguus, -a, -um, watered; irrigare, to water, to irrigate. — Salire (L. 80, N. 10) is used to designate running water. — Lateo, -es, -ere, -ui, to be hidden (cf. in photography the latent image, invisible before development). — For punctum, cf. E. 85, P. 9 and note. It is amusing to see that here Frontinus considers punctum as a word of slang of the fountain-makers. — Silex, -icis, m., hard stone (like flint), pavement. — Meare, to pass, to circulate; (per)meabilis, -is, -e, where one can pass (through). — (Con)vulnerare, to wound, to damage, cf. fr. vulnérable. — Contemno, -is, -ere, tempsi, temptum, to scorn; contemptor, he who scorns. — Leniter, adv., from lenis, -e, gentle (to the touch). — Tueor, -eris, -eri, tuitus sum, to have under the eyes (cf. intueri, to look at), to watch over. Derivative: tutela, -ae, f., defence, tutelage. — Praesto, -as, -are, stiti, stitum, literally, to stand in front, whence to carry it off, to be preferable. Is here employed in the impersonal form.

latin: LXIV — ...Nunc ponam quid ipse scrupulosa inquisitione in commentariis invenerim...
Plus in distributione quam in accepto computabatur quinariis 1263 (mille ducentis sexaginta tribus).
Hujus rei admiratio non mediocriter me convertit ad scrutandum quem ad modum amplius erogaretur quam in patrimonio, ut ita dicam, esset.
Ante omnia itaque capita ductuum metiri adgressus sum, sed longe ampliorem quam in commentariis modum inveni...
LXXIV — Mensuris actis, illud detegitur: 10 000 (decem milia) quinariarum intercidisse, dum beneficia sua principes secundum modum in commentariis adscriptum temperant...
LXXV — Cujus rei causa est fraus aquariorum, quos aquas ex ductibus publicis in privatorum usus derivare deprehendimus,
sed et plerique possessores, quorum agris aqua circumducitur, formas rivorum perforant...
LXXVI — Inriguos agros, tabernas, cenacula etiam, corruptelas denique, omnes perpetuis salientibus instructas invenimus...
CXV — Etiam ille aquariorum tollendus est reditus quem vocant «puncta».
Longa ac diversa sunt spatia per quae fistulae tota meant urbe latentes sub silice.
Has comperi per eum qui adpellabatur «a punctis», passim convulneratas, omnibus in transitu negotiationibus praebuisse peculiaribus fistulis aquam.
Quo efficiebatur ut exiguus modus ad usus publicos perveniret...
CXXX — Legis contemptores non negaverim dignos poena quae intenditur, sed neglegentia longi temporis deceptos leniter revocari oportuit.
In reliquum vero opto ne exsecutio legis necessaria sit, cum officii fidem etiam per offensas tueri praestiterit.
english: ... Now I am going to [set out] what I myself have found in the registers by a scrupulous search...
One counted in the distribution 1,263 quinaries (cf. note) more [than] one had counted at reception!
[My] astonishment at this thing incited me not [a little] (moderately) to research in what way more was drawn than there was [in] the patrimony, so to speak...
So, before everything, I undertook to measure the [inlets] (heads) of the conduits, but I found there a quantity [far greater than in the] registers...

The measurements made, one discovers this: 10,000 quinaries have disappeared on the way, while the [emperors] (princes) regulate their concessions according to the quantity inscribed in the registers...
A cause of this fact is the traffic of the fountain-makers whom we have surprised [diverting] the waters of the public conduits towards private uses,
but also most of the owners of the fields of which [the aqueduct is the boundary] (the water is led around), pierce [the masonry] (the form) of the channels...
We have found watered fields, taverns, shacks also, hovels finally, all of that equipped with running water (all fountains permanent equipped)...
One must also suppress this income of the fountain-makers that they call the «stings».
Long and diverse are the [paths] (spaces) by which the pipes circulate through the whole city, hidden under the pavement.

I discovered that these were pierced here and there (passim) by the one who was called [the officer] «of stings», and that during the passage, by all sorts of combinations, they supplied water to particular [installations] (pipes).
From this it resulted that only a reduced flow reached public uses...

Those who scorn the law, I do not deny [that they are] worthy of the punishment which is prescribed, but those who have been misled (decepti) by a long period of negligence, they must be recalled gently [to order].

[But for the future] (in the rest), I wish that the execution of the law should not be necessary, while it is primordial to safeguard the honesty (fidem) of the function, even by measures of rigour (offensas).
